item.title: Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections
item.description:
White House
Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections
October 21, 20268:09 AM ET
Franco Ordoñez
U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on October 19, 2026 in Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. President Trump is traveling to Kansas for a campaign rally.
Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
President Trump boasted this weekend of his growing power in his second term – and all the things he's doing now that he wouldn't dare in his first term, such as changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
"I don't think I could have done this in my first term," he told supporters in Northern Kentucky, "This is a much more powerful term. I can do stuff that's unbelievable."
He joked about how big companies wouldn't take his call in the first term, but "now they kiss my ass."
Less than two weeks before the election, Trump continues to crash through barriers that he wouldn't dare cross in his first term – and pointing to that power to make his case to midterm voters.

item.title: 2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests
item.description:
Criminal Justice
2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests
October 21, 20265:00 AM ET
Jaclyn Diaz
Police arrest a man as the city of Philadelphia begins a clearing of a drug encampment in the Kensington section of Philadelphia on May 8, 2024.
Spencer Platt/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
hide caption
toggle caption i
Spencer Platt/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, rose in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025 even as rates of violent crime including homicide plummeted to historic national lows, according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us.
Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us, spoke to NPR ahead of the report's release on Wednesday.
"This increase signals a really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the 80s and the 90s," Towns said, referring to the era's tough-on-crime policies, including mandatory minimum prison sentences, that led to a massive rise in incarceration in the U.S. for decades.

item.description:

By
The Associated Press
Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James yells during the second half of an NBA basketball game against the New York Knicks Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, in New York.
Frank Franklin II/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Frank Franklin II/AP
NEW YORK — LeBron James got the business from Knicks fans still gloating and riding an emotional high from an NBA championship banner celebration.
Sports
LeBron James to debut with the Philadelphia 76ers in his 24th NBA season
As he stepped to the free-throw line for the Philadelphia 76ers early in Tuesday night's season opener, Knicks fans erupted toward James with chants of "We don't want you! We don't want you!"
Such a rude reception from New Yorkers to one of the city's newest residents.
The shouts of rejection came in part because there was a plausible scenario under which James would have opened the season at Madison Square Garden in a Knicks uniform.

item.title: FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
item.description:
Business
FAA clears the way for airlines to put Boeing's long-delayed 737 Max 10 into service
October 21, 20262:05 AM ET
By
The Associated Press
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, center, reacts while presenting the certification of Boeing's 737 Max 10 aircraft to Jim Williams, Boeing 737 Development Program chief engineer, at left, and Chris Payne, Boeing Commercial Airplanes vice president and program manager, 737 Development Programs, right, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, at Boeing's factory in Everett, Wash.
Lindsey Wasson/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Lindsey Wasson/AP
Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service Tuesday, ending years of delays.
The 737 Max 10's certification represents another milestone in Boeing's efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers.
